sentences.text: Spiclypeus was a large ceratopsian estimated to have been 4.5 to 6 meters long and weighing about three to four tonnes.
The reconstructed skull of this dinosaur measures 167 centimeters in length.
Its triangular nose horn is 166 millimeters long.
The brow horns measure 228 millimeters on the left side and 246 millimeters on the right.
This species is unique among chasmosaurines for having a wrinkled contact surface on the rear projection of the premaxilla.
It also possesses a distinct combination of sideways-projecting brow horns, fused epiparietals at the base, and specific curling patterns of the front frill horns.
Parallel injuries on the frill suggest the animal survived an attack where a rival's brow horns pierced the shield bone.
The holotype specimen was discovered in September 2005 by Bill D. Shipp on his ranch in Montana.
The land where the fossil was found had been purchased in 2000 by the nuclear physicist Bill D. Shipp.
The excavation team secured all remaining bones of the specimen by 2007.
A severe infection affected the entire lower half of the left humerus, causing dysfunction in the joint surface due to a large abscess.
The body reacted to the humerus infection by remodeling the bone and rotating the joint over 90 degrees from its normal orientation.
Extensive bone remodeling suggests the infection was not immediately lethal and may have been caused by a less virulent form of tuberculosis or fungus.
Spiclypeus is classified within the subfamily Chasmosaurinae.
The dinosaur belongs to the family Ceratopsidae.
Phylogenetic analysis places Spiclypeus as a sister species to a clade containing Kosmoceratops and Vagaceratops, rather than in the Triceratops branch.
Spiclypeus lived between 76.24 and 75.21 million years ago in the lower Coal Ridge Member of the Judith River Formation.
It is debated whether Spiclypeus, Ceratops montanus, and Pentaceratops aquilonius might represent a single species, though this cannot be confirmed due to fragmentary fossils.
